reference.title: heart attack, blood pressure
reference.text: a heart attack = when your heart suddenly stops working properly. blood pressure = how strongly your blood moves around your body; high blood pressure is bad for your heart.

tasks.context:
ARE THEY REALLY GOOD AND BAD?
How do we know what to believe when doctors give us advice about what to drink and what not to drink? Every week, it seems, a scientific study contradicts last week’s research. Jeremy Laurance reviews the latest medical research into drinks.

ALCOHOL
GOOD: For the heart, in small amounts, according to some studies. Two small glasses of red wine a day can cut the risk of heart attack by 30%, especially for middle-aged men.
BAD: For the liver. Liver disease is increasing. Some studies also say that one drink a day increases a woman’s risk of all types of cancer by 6%. Other recent studies suggest that no alcohol at all is the ideal for both men and women.

COFFEE
GOOD: Coffee contains caffeine, which is a stimulant drug, and millions of people drink coffee every day. It improves short-term memory, makes your muscles stronger, keeps you awake, and tastes delicious.
BAD: It’s sometimes connected with heart disease, arthritis, and high blood pressure.

JUICE
GOOD: For people who don’t like fruit and prefer to have it as juice.
BAD: For teeth, especially orange juice which contains a lot of acid. Juice also has a lot of natural sugar, so drinking a lot can add to weight problems.

MILK
GOOD: For very young children, who need the calcium for their bones.
BAD: For adults and older children. They don’t need the extra calcium, and high fat foods like full-fat milk, butter, and cheese can cause heart disease.

TEA
GOOD: Black tea cuts the risk of heart disease. It also reduces stress, makes you more alert, and may help the immune system and prevent diabetes.
BAD: If you add milk, the good effects of tea disappear. Sugar makes it worse.

WATER
GOOD: We can’t live without it, but how much is enough? Typical advice is that you need 2.5 litres a day, but that includes liquid you get from other drinks and from food.
BAD: Too much water can cause problems, e.g. low salt levels. A few people have actually died from drinking too much water.

reference.title: too much, too many, too
rows: I’m very stressed today. I have too much work. My boss talks too much.
too much + uncountable noun, or after a verb
My diet is unhealthy. I eat too many cakes and sweets.
I don’t want to go out tonight. I’m too tired.
too + adjective (NOT I’m too much tired)

reference.title: (not) enough
rows: Do you eat enough vegetables? I don’t drink enough water.
enough before a noun = ‘all that is necessary’
Jane doesn’t sleep enough. She’s always tired.
enough after a verb with no object
Our fridge isn’t big enough for a family of five. I don’t go to bed early enough during the week.
enough after an adjective or adverb

reference.title: a lot / a lot of
reference.text: Use a lot of before a noun: I drink a lot of milk. Use a lot without a noun: My parents don’t drink a lot.
